Building off Malaysia's introduction, I will recall a few key facts about Article IV. Article IV is one of the treaty's fundamental articles. It establishes the treaty as a disarmament treaty. It requires the designation by states parties of an international authority to conduct negotiations, on behalf of States parties with a disarming State, on the terms of its time-bound disarmament plan. It also requires that an international authority be designated to verify the elimination of nuclear weapons by that State. The text of the treaty is not prescriptive in terms of which verification-related activities it requires, but rather the treaty leaves room for verification provisions to be developed that are tailored to a specific context. However, before such time as a former nuclear-armed state joins the Treaty, there are some important decisions that must be taken by States Parties. An informal working group that we co-chair has been tasked on advancing discussions around that. In presenting today's report, I have three points to emphasise which have driven our co-chairs' work on Article IV over the most recent intercessional period. The first point is the process to understand and develop verification protocols under the TPNW will take time and be an holistic endeavour. In our report, we described it as a multi-year mission, as scientific and technical expertise is advanced. Our job as co-chairs has been to approach this role incrementally and to break down the process into achievable steps. A lot of work has already been done internationally on the topic of nuclear disarmament verification, which we have been able to turn to and learn from. Any future disarmament process will be subject to negotiation about the degree of assurance required that the state in question has eliminated its nuclear weapons programme. This will be informed by the nature and complexity of its nuclear weapons programme and the willingness of that state to engage in the process on an ongoing basis. This working group shares the emerging preference among experts for a verification framework that is as simple and as flexible as possible. This does not mean the system won't be intrusive. To the contrary, it likely will be highly intrusive and require inspection regimes to be developed and agreed. My second key point is that verification of nuclear disarmament is indeed possible. in ways that successfully manage the safety, security and non-proliferation concerns. This is increasingly borne out by literature and was certainly the view of all the experts consulted by the co-chairs in this intersessional period. It has also been reiterated by other related expert groups, for example in the IPNDV, the International Partnership for Nuclear Disarmament Verification. Verification is a process common to international treaties. It is a process that allows parties to reassure and build confidence in one another that they are all meeting their obligations. An effective verification system will be one that establishes confidence in compliance of treaty obligations, and the level of verification required will depend on the degree of reassurance required around that state having eliminated its nuclear weapons programme. It is possible to develop a verification framework based on today's systems, tools, and expertise, and it would not require States parties to the Treaty and their representatives gaining access to sensitive nuclear weapons information and data. This issue is common to all NDV discussions. That is, how can States ensure the protection of classified information in order to protect against proliferation risks? To overcome this challenge, a model of disarmament nuclear disarmament verification focused on fissile material has been developed as a possible model for TPNW states parties. That would mean the sharing of sensitive information is not required. Under this model, which has been developed and promoted by experts at UNIDIR and Princeton University, all of a state's fissile material would be moved into a secure area and placed under strict safeguards to be monitored by the IAEA. The disarming state would then open the remainder of its nuclear weapons complex to international inspectors, who would verify the absence of nuclear warheads and fissile material in that, the open sector. At the same time, the disarming state would be responsible for its dismantling process according to a time-bound plan, agreed and verified by the TPNW authority. The TPNW's inspectorate would consistently measure the quantity of fissile material that is mixed down and disposed of over time. comparing that against the state's initial declaration of its quantities of fissile material, with a view to closing the state's material balance. Therefore, no sensitive information would ever need to change hands. This approach has been developed to get around the challenges of authenticity, of information and of secrecy, and is entirely possible when considering nuclear disarmament verification in a state that is totally eliminating its nuclear arsenal. compare that against a state that is engaged in nuclear arms reductions. My third and final point is that nuclear disarmament verification under the TPNW is likely to proceed on the basis of cooperation and not in an adversarial dynamic. This will make the process materially different from the processes outlined in other frameworks, for instance in New START or under the JCPOA. It will take place in a dynamic where nuclear weapons are understood as having no or as having negative value, and the disarming state wishes to demonstrate its commitment to its new identity of being or becoming nuclear-free. Our current understandings of nuclear disarmament verification have their origins in the Cold War arms control processes, characterised by the adversarial relationship between the US and the Soviet Union. This experience has produced several assumptions. namely that verification must be intrusive enough to detect any non-compliance. This has generated a requirement for very high levels of confidence and the ability to detect low levels of non-compliance. However, in that scenario, the States in question continue to see nuclear weapons as having a very high value, and they are engaged in a tense, adversarial relationship. The nuclear disarmament process through the TPNW will not be an extension of nuclear arms control. The underlying assumptions will be different, and the joining States will be looking for opportunities to demonstrate their adherence to the Treaty through a process of active reassurance.
